ladder.why: Plain single-source Dijkstra: settle the smallest tentative distance, relax, skip stale heap entries.
The same Dijkstra on a grid where entering a cell costs its value; four-way moves rule out the simple DP.
Edges cost only 0 or 1, so a deque (front for 0, back for 1) replaces the heap.

ladder.teaches: Bellman-Ford and at most k edges
ladder.why: Bellman-Ford's round i is 'cheapest with at most i edges', so k + 1 rounds enforce the stop limit.
Dijkstra where a path's value is its largest edge: max(d, w) instead of d + w.
The node is not enough; the state (node, discounts used) makes Dijkstra handle the half-price choice.
Dijkstra with products and a max-heap: it works because values never improve along a path.
0-1 BFS with the cost on the departure node instead of the edge.
A minimax path on a grid: the cost is the tallest cell you touch.
Dijkstra first, then dist[u] + w == dist[v] marks the shortest-route edges you build on.
Unlimited tank means you always pay the cheapest price seen so far: state (city, best price).
Multi-source BFS for every cell's distance to a thief, then a maximin path over those values.

notes: Bellman-Ford has only the k-stops form here (no negative-weight problem worth teaching). mt-minimum-obstacles-to-remove-to-allow-figure-fall and uber-minimum-obstacle-removal are not 0-1 BFS despite their names (falling-figure simulation); amazon-minimum-obstacle-removals-on-shortest-grid-path is a monotone-path DP. zorvyn-shortest-path-with-k-free-edges is a good state-Dijkstra problem but has no bounds. citadel-shortest-path-unweighted-graph, amazon-find-minimum-city-hops, benchling-minimum-genetic-mutation and mercor-shortest-path-in-grid-with-obstacles-elimination were moved to graphs (they are BFS).
